title: Lab: automate a real Tier 3 workflow end to end
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Bring the whole month together: design and build an end-to-end automation that detects a real Tier 3 issue, remediates it, reports it, and runs unattended on a schedule.
objectives: Decompose a real Tier 3 workflow into detect, decide, act, and report stages
Combine the module, Graph calls, remediation logic, and a runbook into one solution
Make every action safe with ShouldProcess, retry, and idempotency
Produce a machine-readable report and a human-readable summary
Authenticate the unattended path with a managed identity and least privilege
Define success criteria and a rollback plan for the automation

quiz.q: What is the right first step when automating a Tier 3 workflow end to end?
options: Decompose the workflow into clear stages: detect, decide, act, report
Write the remediation first and test in production
Grant the broadest permissions to avoid errors
Skip dry runs to save time
quiz.why: Breaking the workflow into detect, decide, act, and report stages lets you build and test each piece, add safety at the act stage, and reason about failure before touching the fleet.

quiz.q: Why run the act stage behind ShouldProcess with a pilot ring before fleet-wide rollout?
options: It removes the need for logging
A dry run and small pilot prove the logic and limit blast radius before scaling
quiz.why: Previewing with -WhatIf and piloting on a small group catches mistakes while the impact is tiny, which is essential for high blast-radius endpoint automation.

quiz.q: In the end-to-end design, what authenticates the scheduled, unattended run?
options: The Automation account's managed identity with least-privilege application permissions
quiz.why: Unattended runs use the managed identity granted only the Graph application permissions the workflow needs, removing stored secrets and limiting scope.

quiz.q: Why produce both a machine-readable report (JSON/CSV) and a human-readable summary?
options: The machine format feeds dashboards and tickets while the summary lets a human triage at a glance
Humans cannot read JSON at all
quiz.why: Structured output integrates with downstream systems, and a concise summary makes the run immediately understandable to an on-call engineer, serving two different consumers.

quiz.q: Name two safety mechanisms from this month that your end-to-end automation should include.
quiz.answer: Any two of: ShouldProcess/-WhatIf dry runs, idempotent actions, try/catch error handling, retry with exponential backoff and Retry-After handling, least-privilege scopes, and a pilot ring before fleet rollout.
quiz.why: Production endpoint automation must be previewable, idempotent, resilient to throttling/transient errors, least-privilege, and rolled out gradually — these were the recurring themes of the month.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what should your rollback plan cover for an automation that changes device or group state?
quiz.answer: It should define how to stop the schedule, reverse the change (for example remove added group members or restore the prior policy), and confirm devices returned to the known-good baseline you exported beforehand.
quiz.why: Because changes have blast radius, a tested rollback — disable schedule, reverse the action, verify against the exported baseline — turns a bad run from an incident into a non-event.

slides.title: Lab: automate a real Tier 3 workflow end to end
slides.sub: Month 2 - Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale  |  Lesson 8
slides.narration: This is the capstone of Month Two. Everything you have learned, PowerShell craft, Graph, remediation thinking, modules, safety, and runbooks, comes together to build one real automation end to end. By the end you will have a solution that detects a genuine Tier 3 problem, fixes it safely, reports on it, and runs unattended on a schedule. This is what senior endpoint engineering looks like.

slides.title: The brief
bullets: Find Windows devices not synced in 30 days.
Tag them into a remediation group.
Attempt a sync, then report.
Run it unattended on a schedule.
slides.narration: Here is the brief. You will build one automation that solves a real Tier 3 problem from end to end: find every Windows device that has not synced with Intune in thirty days, tag it into a remediation group, attempt a sync, and produce a report, all running unattended on a schedule. This single lab ties together every skill from the month. Do not try to write it all at once. We decompose it into stages first.

slides.title: Decompose: detect, decide, act, report
bullets: Detect: read the current fleet state.
Decide: the rule for healthy vs unhealthy.
Act: the safe, idempotent change.
Report: machine-readable plus human summary.
slides.narration: The right first move with any end to end workflow is to decompose it into clear stages: detect, decide, act, and report. Detect is read only, gathering the current state. Decide is just the predicate that separates healthy from unhealthy. Act is the change, made safe. And report tells two audiences what happened. Build and test each stage on its own before wiring them together. This decomposition is itself the senior skill, because it lets you reason about failure at each step.

slides.title: Stages 1 and 2: detect and decide
bullets: Read-only: pull the fleet with -All.
Filter server-side for Windows.
Apply the staleness rule as the decide step.
No changes happen yet.
slides.narration: Stages one and two are detect and decide, and they are entirely read only. Pull the fleet with dash All so you miss nothing, filter server side for Windows to keep it fast, and then apply your staleness rule, last sync before the cutoff. The decide stage is just that Where dash Object predicate separating healthy from unhealthy. Nothing changes at this point, which means you can run it against production safely, all day, to size the problem before you act.

slides.title: Stage 3: act, safely
bullets: Every action behind ShouldProcess.
Use the Invoke-WithRetry helper from lesson 6.
Idempotent: re-running creates no duplicates.
Emit a result object per device.
slides.narration: Stage three is where you act, and this is where all the safety lives. Every action goes behind P S Cmdlet dot Should Process so you get a dash WhatIf dry run. Wrap the Graph calls in the Invoke dash With Retry helper from lesson six so transient failures and throttling are handled. Make it idempotent, so adding a device already in the group and syncing again causes no harm. And emit a result object per device, recording whether it was remediated or failed and why. Catch errors per device so one bad device does not abort the whole run.

slides.title: Stage 4: report for two audiences
bullets: Machine-readable JSON or CSV for systems.
Feeds dashboards and ticket creation.
One-line human summary for on-call triage.
Counts: remediated, failed, total.
slides.code:
$report | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 | Set-Content '.\stale-report.json'
$ok  = ($report | ? Action -eq 'Remediated').Count
$bad = ($report | ? Action -eq 'Failed').Count
Write-Output "Run: $ok remediated, $bad failed, $($report.Count) total"
slides.narration: Stage four is reporting, and you serve two different audiences. Produce a machine readable artefact, J S O N or C S V, that downstream systems can ingest to feed dashboards and open tickets automatically. And produce a human readable one line summary so an on call engineer can triage the run at a glance: so many remediated, so many failed, so many total. Both come from the same per device result objects you built in stage three. Two formats, two consumers, one source of truth.

slides.title: Make it unattended
bullets: Wrap the flow in an Azure Automation runbook.
Authenticate with Connect-MgGraph -Identity.
Grant least-privilege application permissions.
Pin modules, schedule daily, pilot with -WhatIf first.
slides.narration: Finally, make it unattended. Wrap the whole flow in an Azure Automation runbook that authenticates with Connect dash M g Graph dash Identity, using the managed identity so there are no secrets. Grant that identity only the application permissions the workflow needs, Device Management Managed Devices Read Write All and Group Read Write All, and nothing more. Pin your module versions, attach a daily schedule, and crucially, pilot on a small ring with dash WhatIf before you ever let it run fleet wide. Preview first, scale last.

slides.title: Success criteria and rollback
bullets: Define what success looks like before you run.
Have a tested rollback: disable, reverse, verify.
Rollback restores the exported baseline.
A rollback turns a bad run into a non-event.
slides.code:
# Rollback: disable schedule ->
#   Remove-MgGroupMemberByRef for added devices ->
#   verify against exported baseline
slides.narration: Two things separate professional automation from a risky script. First, define your success criteria before you run, so you know whether it worked. Second, have a tested rollback plan, because anything that changes device or group state has blast radius. Your rollback should disable the schedule, reverse the change, removing the devices you added to the group, and verify the fleet is back to the baseline you exported beforehand. A bad run with a tested rollback is a non event. A bad run without one is an incident.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Decompose: detect, decide, act, report.
Safety everywhere: WhatIf, retry, idempotency, least privilege.
Two report formats; unattended via managed identity.
Define success criteria and a rollback plan.
Task: deliver the full solution as one reviewable package.
slides.narration: Let us recap the whole month in one workflow. Decompose into detect, decide, act, and report. Put safety everywhere: dash WhatIf dry runs, retry with backoff, idempotent actions, and least privilege permissions. Report in two formats, and run it unattended with a managed identity. And always define success criteria and a tested rollback. Your task: deliver the complete solution as one reviewable package. A read only detect function and decide rule, an act function with Should Process, retry, and idempotency emitting per device results, a report stage with J S O N and a summary, a runbook wrapper with managed identity, pinned modules, and a schedule, and a short operations runbook covering the exact least privilege permissions, your WhatIf pilot, success criteria, and a tested rollback. Prove a second run is idempotent and remediates nothing already healthy. That is Month Two complete. Outstanding work, and I will see you in Month Three.
